draft.title: Hypothetical Prompt Regression Test Design: Fixed Prompts & Controlled Comparison
draft.body: I'm outlining a hypothetical approach for a prompt regression test suite. The core idea is to evaluate prompt changes systematically. We'd use a fixed set of 12 test prompts [F1], designed to include both answerable questions and cases with insufficient information [F3]. The proposed method involves comparing an 'old' prompt against a 'new' one using the exact same model settings and parameters on identical hardware [F2]. This controlled comparison aims to isolate the impact of prompt modifications. It is crucial to understand that this is a conceptual design; no actual results or improvements have been measured or are available at this stage [F4]. The goal is to discuss the methodology itself. What are your thoughts on this structured approach to prompt testing?

draft.title: Hypothetical Prompt Regression Testing Framework: Input and Comparison Strategy
draft.body: I'm proposing a hypothetical framework for designing prompt regression tests for local LLMs. The methodology centers on a controlled comparison using a predefined set of 12 test prompts [F1]. This set is designed to include questions with clear answers and others where the provided information is insufficient [F3]. The core of the test would be to run both an existing prompt and a modified version against the same model, under identical settings and parameters [F2]. This controlled environment is intended to allow for a direct comparison of prompt performance. It is vital to reiterate that this is a hypothetical experimental design; no actual measurements or results are available at this time [F4]. The aim is to gather feedback on the proposed testing structure.

draft.title: Hypothetical Prompt Regression Testing: Design Considerations
draft.body: This post outlines a hypothetical framework for designing a prompt regression test suite for local LLMs. The objective is to establish a repeatable method for evaluating prompt efficacy without relying on pre-existing results. We propose using a fixed set of 12 test prompts, covering both directly answerable questions and cases where information is insufficient. The core idea is to compare the output of an old prompt against a new variant using identical model settings and parameters on the same hardware. This controlled comparison is crucial for isolating the impact of prompt changes. It's important to note that this is a conceptual design, and no actual performance improvements or measurements have been conducted or are available at this stage. The goal is to solicit feedback on the proposed testing methodology itself, before any implementation or data collection occurs. What are your thoughts on structuring such a test?
